content.en:
Developing nations face a structural challenge in funding scientific research, relying heavily on government spending rather than private sector R&D.

  • Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD): Most developing nations spend less than 1% of their GDP on R&D (e.g., India ~0.65%, Brazil ~1.2%). Developed nations like South Korea and the US spend 3% to 4.8%.
  • Funding Source Mismatch: In developed nations, the private sector contributes over 70% of R&D funding. In developing nations, the government remains the primary funder (~60% in India), leading to bureaucratic delays and lower commercialization rates.
  • Brain Drain: The migration of highly trained scientific talent to developed economies due to better research infrastructure and higher salaries, causing a severe human capital loss.

content.en:
The global intellectual property regime can act as a double-edged sword, incentivizing global innovation while locking out poorer nations from vital technologies.

  • North-South Technology Transfer: The flow of advanced technology from developed industrial nations (Global North) to developing ones (Global South). Often constrained by high licensing costs and restrictive terms.
  • TRIPS Agreement Constraints: The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights mandates strict patent enforcement, which can increase the cost of essential seeds and pharmaceuticals in developing nations.
  • Compulsory Licensing & Evergreening: Developing nations utilize flexibilities like Compulsory Licensing (producing patented life-saving drugs locally during emergencies) and legal clauses preventing patent evergreening (such as Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act) to safeguard public interest.

S&T Indicators: Developed vs. Developing Nations

Indicator Developed Nations (Global North) Developing Nations (Global South)
GERD as % of GDP High (2.5% to 4.8%) Low (Typically < 1%)
Primary R&D Funder Private Sector (70%+) Public Sector/Government (60%+)
IPR Strategy Focus Strict enforcement, evergreening, high licensing fees Flexibilities, generic manufacturing, compulsory licensing
Innovation Model Frontier R&D (breakthrough technologies) Adaptive R&D (reverse engineering, appropriate tech)

content.en:
Developing nations can accelerate development by adopting non-linear paths of technological acquisition.

  • Technology Leapfrogging: Bypassing intermediate stages of technology to adopt the latest frontier systems (e.g., skipping landline telephony straight to mobile broadband, skipping physical branch banking to mobile UPI).
  • Appropriate/Intermediate Technology: S&T systems that are decentralized, low-cost, resource-efficient, and easily maintainable using local skills (e.g., gravity-fed water purifiers, solar-powered farm pumps).

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is the main objective of Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970?
opts: To allow evergreening of pharmaceutical patents.
To prevent the patenting of mere discoveries or minor modifications of known substances.
To ban all foreign pharmaceutical companies from selling drugs in India.
To automatically grant compulsory licenses to all local firms.
practiceQuestions.sol: Section 3(d) prevents evergreening by stating that minor modifications of known substances without significant increase in efficacy are not patentable.

practiceQuestions.q: The Addis Ababa Action Agenda of 2015 led to the creation of which of the following UN mechanisms to aid developing nations?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Technology Facilitation Mechanism (TFM) was established to support the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by facilitating technology transfer and access.

practiceQuestions.q: In most developing countries, the largest share of funding for scientific R&D (GERD) comes from:
practiceQuestions.sol: Unlike developed countries where the private sector leads R&D funding, developing nations rely heavily on government and public funding (~60%+).

practiceQuestions.q: The practice of bypassing older, intermediate technologies to adopt advanced modern technologies directly is known as:
practiceQuestions.sol: Technology leapfrogging allows developing nations to skip developmental stages (like copper telephone wires) and jump straight to advanced technologies (like mobile networks).

practiceQuestions.q: Who authored the book 'Small is Beautiful', establishing the core principles of Appropriate Technology?
practiceQuestions.sol: E.F. Schumacher popularized appropriate technology in his 1973 book, advocating for decentralized, cheap, and labor-intensive solutions.

practiceQuestions.q: Compulsory Licensing, as defined under the WTO TRIPS agreement, allows a government to:
opts: Abolish all intellectual property rights within the country.
Grant a license to a local company to produce a patented product without the patent owner's consent during emergencies.
Import counterfeit goods without tariff penalties.
practiceQuestions.sol: Compulsory licensing is a TRIPS flexibility that permits governments to authorize local production of patented drugs during health crises.

practiceQuestions.q: The emigration of highly skilled scientists, engineers, and doctors from developing nations to developed economies is termed:
practiceQuestions.sol: Brain drain refers to the loss of educated and skilled human capital from developing nations seeking better opportunities abroad.

practiceQuestions.q: When a developing country returns highly educated migrants back to their home country to start high-tech businesses, it is experiencing:
practiceQuestions.sol: Brain circulation or brain gain refers to the return of skilled professionals bringing back capital, knowledge, and technology to their home countries.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is a key attribute of 'Appropriate Technology'?
opts: Relies on local resources, labor-intensive, and simple to maintain
Requires high licensing fees from developed nations
practiceQuestions.sol: Appropriate technology focuses on local solutions that fit the low-capital, high-labor availability of developing regions.

practiceQuestions.q: India's Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD) as a percentage of GDP is approximately:
practiceQuestions.sol: India spends a relatively low percentage of its GDP on R&D, hovering between 0.6% and 0.8%.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following international agreements governs global standards for patents, copyrights, and trademarks under the WTO?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) is the key WTO agreement regulating global IPR standards.

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Digital Divide' refers to the inequality in access to:
practiceQuestions.sol: The digital divide is the gap between demographics and regions that have access to modern ICT and those that don't.

practiceQuestions.q: M-Pesa in Kenya is a classic example of technology leapfrogging in which sector?
practiceQuestions.sol: M-Pesa allowed millions of Kenyans to skip physical brick-and-mortar banking and jump straight to mobile phone-based financial transactions.

practiceQuestions.q: Which Indian organization manages and operates the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) technology platform?
practiceQuestions.sol: The NPCI is an umbrella organization for operating retail payments and settlement systems in India, including UPI.

practiceQuestions.q: The use of satellite data, GPS, and IoT sensors to optimize water and fertilizer use in developing agriculture is called:
practiceQuestions.sol: Precision farming uses S&T to ensure crops receive exactly what they need for optimum health and productivity.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is a primary barrier to North-South technology transfer?
opts: Low interest in technology among developing countries
High licensing costs and strict IPR protectionism by developed nations
The complete absence of international trade channels
A global ban on scientific publications
practiceQuestions.sol: Developed nations often guard their proprietary technologies with high patent fees and strict conditions, hindering transfer to poorer nations.

practiceQuestions.q: The process of analyzing a foreign device or software to discover its design and duplicate it with local modifications is called:
practiceQuestions.sol: Reverse engineering has historically been a tool for developing nations (like East Asian economies) to copy and adapt technology.

practiceQuestions.q: The concept of 'Technological Dualism' in developing nations refers to the coexistence of:
opts: Military and civilian space research programs
A highly advanced modern tech sector and a backward traditional sector
Public and private funding in equal proportions
practiceQuestions.sol: Technological dualism describes the split where high-tech urban hubs (e.g., Bengaluru IT parks) coexist alongside traditional, low-tech rural areas.

practiceQuestions.q: Which UN organization is primarily responsible for promoting international intellectual property protection?
practiceQuestions.sol: The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) is the UN agency dedicated to using intellectual property to encourage innovation.

practiceQuestions.q: A pool of patents shared among several organizations to facilitate collaborative R&D and avoid litigation is called a:
practiceQuestions.sol: Patent pooling allows multiple entities to share technologies, which is especially useful for developing vaccines or clean energy.

practiceQuestions.q: Which S&T intervention led to self-sufficiency in food grain production in India during the late 1960s?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Green Revolution introduced High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilizers, and advanced irrigation S&T to Indian agriculture.

practiceQuestions.q: Why is the private sector R&D expenditure low in most developing economies?
opts: Private companies are legally banned from doing research.
High market uncertainty, low capital availability, and focus on short-term trading profits.
Developing country governments fund 100% of private salaries.
Complete lack of consumer interest in new products.
practiceQuestions.sol: Private firms in developing countries often prefer low-risk, immediate commercial activities rather than long-term, high-risk capital investment in R&D.

practiceQuestions.q: The Doha Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement (2001) clarified that:
opts: TRIPS should be interpreted in a way that supports public health and access to medicines.
Developing nations must stop producing generic medicines entirely.
All patents on pharmaceuticals are abolished.
Developed nations are banned from selling medical technology.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Doha Declaration affirmed that TRIPS does not and should not prevent members from taking measures to protect public health.

practiceQuestions.q: Which S&T sector in India has historically shown the highest indigenous success due to international sanctions?
practiceQuestions.sol: Sanctions and technology denials (e.g., denial of cryogenic engines) forced organizations like ISRO and BARC to develop indigenous technologies.

practiceQuestions.q: A decentralized solar-powered micro-grid in a rural Indian village is an example of:
practiceQuestions.sol: A local, low-cost solar grid is appropriate because it uses clean energy and fits the rural infrastructure gap.

practiceQuestions.q: What is the primary risk of relying entirely on foreign technology transfer for national development?
opts: High tech dependency, vulnerability to sanctions, and lack of local S&T skill development
Immediate increase in direct income tax
Complete closure of all local retail markets
Over-supply of skilled domestic R&D jobs
practiceQuestions.sol: Without indigenous S&T development, countries remain dependent on foreign intellectual property and vulnerable to geopolitical sanctions.

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'South-South Cooperation' in S&T refers to collaboration between:
opts: Developed countries located in the southern hemisphere
Developing nations to share appropriate technologies and skills
practiceQuestions.sol: South-South S&T cooperation helps developing countries share low-cost, adaptive technologies suited for similar socio-economic conditions.

practiceQuestions.q: The UN Technology Bank for Least Developed Countries was created to:
opts: Strengthen S&T capabilities and facilitate technology transfer in the poorest nations
Provide free smartphones to all citizens
practiceQuestions.sol: The UN Tech Bank aims to help Least Developed Countries (LDCs) build their S&T capacities and access technology.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is a negative impact of brain drain on a developing nation?
opts: Loss of taxpayers' money spent on subsidized higher education for migrated professionals
Immediate reduction in the rate of inflation
practiceQuestions.sol: When highly subsidized professionals (e.g., IIT/AIIMS graduates) migrate, the home country loses both its fiscal investment and elite human capital.

practiceQuestions.q: Which Indian policy framework outlines the national vision for science, technology, and innovation?
opts: STI Policy (Science, Technology, and Innovation Policy)
practiceQuestions.sol: The Science, Technology, and Innovation Policy (STIP) guides India's funding, direction, and execution of R&D.

practiceQuestions.q: A low-cost gravity-based water filter that requires no electricity is classified as:
practiceQuestions.sol: It is low-cost, uses gravity, requires no power, and serves local public health needs directly.

practiceQuestions.q: The WTO agreement that sets the minimum standards for intellectual property regulation is:
practiceQuestions.sol: TRIPS is the primary WTO agreement setting rules for global IPR enforcement.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is a key feature of the 'India Stack' digital public infrastructure?
opts: Open API architecture allowing private sector innovation on top of government systems
High transaction fees for user registrations
practiceQuestions.sol: India Stack uses open APIs to let businesses and governments build services (like UPI, e-KYC) on top of public digital infrastructure.

practiceQuestions.q: What does GERD stand for in science and technology policy?
opts: Gross Domestic Expenditure on Research and Development
Generic Enforcement of Rights and Patents
practiceQuestions.sol: GERD is the standard global indicator for tracking total national research and development spending.

practiceQuestions.q: Which country spends the highest absolute amount on R&D globally?
practiceQuestions.sol: The United States is the largest spender on R&D in absolute terms, followed closely by China.

practiceQuestions.q: The introduction of genetically modified Bt Cotton in India is an example of S&T application in:
practiceQuestions.sol: Bt Cotton is a genetically modified pest-resistant crop representing agricultural S&T application.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes 'Evergreening' of patents?
opts: Extending the monopoly life of a patent by making minor, non-therapeutic modifications to an old drug.
Offering lifetime patents for space research.
Banning patents on all natural plants.
practiceQuestions.sol: Evergreening is a strategy where companies file successive minor patents to prolong monopoly prices on drugs.

practiceQuestions.q: Which term refers to the return of skilled professionals to their home country, bringing back global networks and expertise?
practiceQuestions.sol: Reverse brain drain or brain circulation describes the return of skilled talent, benefiting the native country.

practiceQuestions.q: The use of drones to map village land properties in India under the SVAMITVA scheme represents:
opts: S&T application in rural governance and land reforms
practiceQuestions.sol: SVAMITVA uses drone technology to map rural land parcels, improving property titling and governance.

practiceQuestions.q: The main concern of developing countries regarding TRIPS rules on agricultural seeds is:
opts: A complete ban on planting wheat.
Patent controls by multinational corporations preventing seed saving and raising farming costs.
The mandatory export of all domestic crops.
Too many free seeds distributed by the WTO.
practiceQuestions.sol: Patenting seeds allows corporate giants to restrict farmers from saving and reusing seeds, which threatens food security.

practiceQuestions.q: Which S&T sector handles the development of generic medicines in developing nations?
practiceQuestions.sol: Generic pharmaceuticals provide affordable bio-equivalent copies of off-patent drugs in developing nations.

practiceQuestions.q: The transition from traditional bank books to smartphone UPI apps in India is an example of:
practiceQuestions.sol: India bypassed the credit card transition stage, moving directly to mobile banking and instant UPI.

practiceQuestions.q: Which organization is the UN focal point for science and technology for development?
opts: UN CSTD (Commission on Science and Technology for Development)
practiceQuestions.sol: The CSTD is a subsidiary body of ECOSOC, serving as the UN focal point for S&T policy advice.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is a positive impact of R&D cooperation among BRICS nations?
opts: Enhancing South-South technology transfer and joint space/energy research
Banning private tech companies in all member states
Applying strict Western patent codes immediately
Allowing only US Dollar currency for all R&D projects
practiceQuestions.sol: BRICS R&D cooperation strengthens South-South technology transfer and collaborative research on shared development challenges.

practiceQuestions.q: A solar water heater built using local materials in a village is an example of:
practiceQuestions.sol: It is low-cost, customized, locally built, and fits the local energy access needs.

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Intellectual Property Right' excludes which of the following?
practiceQuestions.sol: Natural minerals are physical natural resources; IPRs apply only to creations of the human mind.

practiceQuestions.q: Which Indian state has a dedicated department for Science & Technology to coordinate state-level R&D?
opts: Almost all Indian states have State Councils for S&T
practiceQuestions.sol: DST coordinates with State Councils for Science & Technology in almost all states to promote local R&D.

practiceQuestions.q: A patent is valid for how many years globally under the TRIPS agreement?
practiceQuestions.sol: TRIPS sets a mandatory minimum patent protection period of 20 years from the filing date.

practiceQuestions.q: A technology that is imported from a developed country but requires expensive foreign engineers to operate and maintain is:
opts: Inappropriate technology due to lack of local capacity development
practiceQuestions.sol: If a technology requires foreign expertise and cannot be managed locally, it creates high dependency, failing the test of appropriate technology.

practiceQuestions.q: Which S&T platform supports digital identification of all Indian residents?
practiceQuestions.sol: Aadhaar is a 12-digit unique identity number issued by UIDAI, serving as a core digital identity DPI.

fact.en: Trap 1: Evergreening of Patents: TRIPS mandates 20-year patents. Developing countries (e.g., India under Section 3(d) of Patents Act) block **evergreening** (securing minor variations of existing drugs to extend patents). Beware of assumptions that all countries permit patent extensions for minor chemical modifications.

Beware of assumptions that all countries permit patent extensions for minor chemical modifications.

fact.en: Trap 2: Technology Leapfrogging: Leapfrogging doesn't mean skipping scientific research. It means bypassing physical developmental infrastructure (e.g., landline phone lines) to jump straight to advanced technologies (e.g., mobile networks, digital payment DPI).

fact.en: Trap 3: GERD/GDP Ratio: While India is a major space and software power, its Gross Expenditure on R&D (GERD) sits low at ~0.65% of GDP, compared to 2.5-4.8% in developed nations. Do not assume high absolute S&T output matches a high R&D-to-GDP investment ratio.
